opus-5.5.text:
I think the culture is probably the thing I'm proudest of, honestly, more than any single result.

From the start there was a strong belief that robotics had been held back partly because the field was fragmented. Every lab had its own robot, its own task, its own small dataset, and people optimized for a demo that worked once on camera. So the culture we tried to build was the opposite: think in terms of general models, shared data, and shared infrastructure. Nobody owns "their" robot or "their" task. If you improve the data pipeline or the training recipe, everyone benefits, and that's valued as much as a flashy result.

The second thing is that it's very hands-on. Researchers aren't separate from the robots. People who write the model code also go to the floor, watch the robot fail, look at the data, and talk to the operators collecting demonstrations. A lot of real insight in robotics comes from staring at failure cases, not from the loss curve. So there's a norm that you should be close to reality.

Third, there's a lot of intellectual honesty. In robotics it's easy to fool yourself: you cherry-pick a rollout, or the evaluation setup quietly changes. We put a lot of weight on careful evaluation and on saying clearly when something doesn't work. Negative results get shared internally, and that saves everyone a lot of time.

And finally, it's quite flat and low-ego. There are very senior people and people fresh out of school working side by side, and the best idea wins regardless of who it comes from. People are there because they believe general-purpose robot intelligence is possible within our careers. That shared conviction makes it feel less like a company and more like a long research mission we're all on together.

r002.rationale: It presents shared data and infrastructure, collaboration across tasks, and internal sharing of negative results as defining parts of the culture, communicating an open research atmosphere.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the first thing to say is that the culture wasn't really designed from the top down. It grew out of the kind of people who showed up in the first year. Most of us came from research labs, and a lot of us had spent years on problems where you could run an experiment overnight and look at a number in the morning. Robotics is not like that. You spend half your day debugging a cable, or waiting for someone to reset a scene, or realizing the gripper is slightly bent. So the first cultural trait that formed was patience mixed with a certain stubbornness. People who need constant fast feedback tend to leave quickly, and the ones who stay are the ones who can sit with a problem that fights back physically.

The second thing is that there is very little separation between "research people" and "robot people." At a lot of places there's a hierarchy where the person writing the paper is a tier above the person collecting data. We tried hard not to have that. Everyone teleoperates. Everyone has spent hours folding laundry with a robot arm. Partly that's practical, because you simply can't understand the failure modes of a policy if you've never felt how the arm moves, but it also keeps people honest. If you have to collect the data yourself, you stop pretending that scaling it is a trivial detail.

Third, we are very demo-driven in a way that sometimes surprises outsiders. Internally, the unit of progress isn't a benchmark number, it's whether the robot can actually do the thing in a kitchen that it has never seen. That creates a kind of healthy skepticism toward our own results. A plot can lie to you. A robot putting a dish in the rack either happens or it doesn't, and the whole team is in the room watching. There's a lot of laughing at failures, which I think matters. If people are scared of a robot failing in public, they'll quietly cherry-pick, and the whole research program rots.

And honestly, the last piece is that we're still small enough that there's not much politics. People argue about ideas loudly and then go get coffee together. I don't know how long that survives as we grow. That's the thing I think about most, how you keep the "everyone touches the robot" ethos when you're two or three times the size.

r002.rationale: It describes little separation between research and robot work, no hierarchy, and people arguing openly about ideas, conveying a relatively open research atmosphere.

astra-6.text: I think the culture is still taking shape. The kind of culture I’d want us to build is one where people can be ambitious and also very honest about what’s working and what isn’t. You need room to pursue an idea that might sound a little crazy, but you also need to be comfortable saying, “We tried it, and the evidence isn’t there yet.” To me, those two things reinforce each other. People can take bigger risks when changing their mind is treated as part of the work.

sol-6.1.text:
I think culture shows up most clearly in how people work together when they don’t know the answer. With physical intelligence, you’re constantly dealing with that uncertainty. You have an idea, you try it on a robot, and the result can challenge an assumption you didn’t even realize you were making.

The culture I value is one where people can be ambitious about the goal and very honest about what’s actually working. You want people to share failures early, ask basic questions, and help each other understand what happened. That makes the work feel like a shared scientific effort, where changing your mind is part of making progress.
